title: Responding to Incidents
objective: Can carry out a defensive response that includes preparation, containment, evidence preservation, recovery, and learning.

sections.title: Make the Response Plan Actionable
paragraphs: The response plan defines contacts, permissions, severity, evidence preservation, isolation decisions, business continuity, external communications, recovery, and lessons learned. To avoid searching for necessary permissions or procedures for the first time during an actual incident, validate the runbooks and access in advance.

During exercises, measure more than whether the exercise succeeded: measure how long it takes detection results to reach the responsible personnel, whether the scope of impact can be limited, whether evidence can be preserved, and whether the recovery procedures work. Feed the exercise results back into the plan instead of relying solely on the personnel’s memory.

sections.title: Sequencing Containment, Preservation, and Recovery
paragraphs: When responding to a security event, balance actions that limit the impact with actions that preserve evidence. Isolate only the affected accounts, roles, network paths, and credentials to the minimum extent necessary, and record the actions taken, the time, and the reasons for the decisions.

Deleting evidence, disabling logs, or making overly broad bulk changes may appear to speed recovery, but these actions make it more difficult to identify the root cause and conduct an audit. After containment, review the change history, credentials, configurations, and data access, then restore the environment to a state that meets the recovery criteria.

sources.label: SCS-C03 Exam Guide: Responding to Security Events

sections.title: Connecting Post-Incident Reviews to Stronger Defenses
paragraphs: In a post-incident review, we examine not to assign individual blame, but to determine where defenses worked and where they were delayed across detection, notification, decision-making, authorization, isolation, recovery, and communication. Based on the supporting timeline and change records, we establish the owners and completion criteria for measures to prevent recurrence.

Improvement measures are not limited to adding detection rules. We prioritize least privilege, secret rotation, network boundaries, backups, runbooks, and exercise frequency according to risk and impact.

checkpoints.prompt: The team responding to a finding involving suspected credential misuse wants to verify the effectiveness of its procedures in advance. Which preparation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Do not verify permissions and procedures until an actual incident occurs.
choices.explanation: This can cause response delays and insufficient permissions.

choices.text: Do not keep logs during the exercise; share the results only verbally.
choices.explanation: This leaves no evidence needed for improvement.

choices.text: Exercise a runbook covering contacts, permissions, isolation, evidence preservation, and recovery, and record response times and gaps.
choices.explanation: This verifies the preparation and improvement areas needed for an actual response.

checkpoints.prompt: The 20 EC2 workers that process orders use the same IAM role. During the investigation, the incident response team found that suspicious communication was continuing from just one worker. The other 19 are operating normally, and there is currently no evidence that the credentials have been used elsewhere. While continuing to process orders, how far should you isolate the environment first?

choices.text: Immediately revoke all existing sessions for the shared IAM role and restart the 20 workers.
choices.explanation: Revoking the shared role's sessions indiscriminately could prevent even the healthy workers from continuing to process orders.

choices.text: Isolate the affected worker from order processing and normal network communication, leaving only the routes required for the investigation. Preserve logs and execution traces, and continue monitoring for any external use of the credentials.
choices.explanation: Isolating only the communicating worker first allows the investigation to continue without stopping the healthy workers. If credential leakage is confirmed, contain the credentials as well.

choices.text: Immediately delete the affected worker and use logs from the healthy workers for the investigation.
choices.explanation: Deleting the worker could destroy evidence needed to determine the cause, including its memory and logs that have not yet been collected.

checkpoints.prompt: The same type of misconfiguration recurred after the incident. Which improvement is most appropriate?

choices.text: Determine the cause solely from stakeholders’ memories and leave no records.
choices.explanation: This does not produce a verifiable improvement.

choices.text: Based on the timeline and change records, identify gaps in detection, permissions, configuration, and runbooks, then break them down into actions with owners and completion criteria.
choices.explanation: This connects specific points of failure in the defenses to concrete measures for preventing recurrence.

choices.text: Delete the relevant detection to reduce the number of notifications.
choices.explanation: This would eliminate early detection of a recurrence.
